story.title: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
story.text: CISA Adds Two Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. - CVE-2026-133968 Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal Vulnerability - CVE-2026-134624 N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance. This product is provided subject to this Notification and this Privacy & Use policy.

content.what_happened: CISA added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog based on evidence of active exploitation: CVE-2026-133968 (Project MONAI MONAI Label Path Traversal) and CVE-2026-134624 (N-able Mail Assure SSRF).
content.who_affected: Federal Civilian Executive Branch agencies and other organizations using Project MONAI or N-able Mail Assure (SpamExperts) products.
content.what_changed: BOD 26-04 now requires FCEB agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of these KEV Catalog vulnerabilities on publicly exposed assets and to check for prior compromise before patching.
content.mitigation: Organizations should apply available patches and monitor for exploitation, with FCEB agencies required to remediate high-risk KEV vulnerabilities on exposed assets promptly.

history.title: Hackers Exploit Critical VMware, Cisco, and Apache Flaws as Espionage Attacks Emerge
history.text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Friday added four flaws impacting Apache Roller, Cisco Expressway, SAP NetWeaver, and Broadcom VMware vCenter to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV), citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerabilities are listed below - - CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Apache Roller that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via the XML-RPC endpoint, which accepts and deserializes vendor extension types before authentication. (Fixed in November 2026) - CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A use of hard-coded credentials vulnerability in Cisco Expressway Series that could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with persistent cookies and network access to execute commands as root on a clustered device via the database service. (Fixed in October 2026) - CVE-2025-42884 (CVSS score: 6.5) - An improper neutralization of special elements in data query logic vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to disclose or modify server information via injected JNDI environment properties or a URL used during JNDI lookup operations. (Fixed in November 2025) - CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel vulnerability in VMware vCenter that could allow an unauthenticated attacker with network access to vCenter to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. (Fixed in November 2026) Earlier this week, the maintainers of Apache Roller acknowledged that the "issue is being actively exploited" but did not reveal how it was being weaponized or who is behind it. As of writing, there also appear to be no public reports documenting active exploitation of CVE-2025-42884. The addition of CVE-2026-76466 to the KEV catalog follows a report from F6 that the vulnerability was exploited to breach a Russian organization following the release of a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit, enabling the attackers to move laterally across the network and access sensitive data. The activity has not been attributed to any threat actor. The exploitation of CVE-2026-123890, on the other hand, has linked to a suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221), which is said to have weaponized it in conjunction with another now-patched flaw in BeyondTrust Remote Support (CVE-2026-102764, CVSS score: 9.3) to deploy custom backdoors for persistent access and data theft. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have been urged to patch all four vulnerabilities by November 23, 2026, pursuant to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

history.title: Microsoft Entra Connect Health flaw exploited to steal tenant data
history.text: Microsoft is warning organizations that it suffered a data breach after attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Entra Connect Health service to gain unauthorized access to administrator email addresses and tenant configuration information. Microsoft Entra Connect Health is a cloud-based monitoring service that allows administrators to monitor the health, performance, and alerts of their on-premises identity infrastructure through the Microsoft Entra admin center. According to a security notification sent to admins yesterday and shared on Reddit, Microsoft discovered the vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API on November 9, 2026, after it was first introduced on July 23. An investigation determined that the flaw was exploited, allowing unauthorized parties to access tenant and service-monitoring metadata and potentially modify Connect Health monitoring configurations. "On 20 November 2026, we concluded our investigation and determined that unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata associated with your organization had occurred. We did not identify any unauthorized configuration changes," Microsoft said in the notification. The company says the exposed information included: - Email addresses belonging to tenant technical contacts and administrator accounts. - Tenant IDs, display names, initial domain names, country codes, and regional information. - Microsoft Entra license tiers and directory synchronization status, including whether synchronization was enabled and the last synchronization timestamp. - Connect Health onboarding status. - An expired certificate previously used to register Connect Health agents with a Microsoft internal service that was decommissioned in late 2024. Microsoft says the expired certificate was no longer in use but remained in Connect Health storage and was still returned by the API. However, the company says the vulnerability did not expose user passwords, password hashes, authentication tokens, valid cryptographic keys, on-premises server and Active Directory topology details, or Azure subscription information. Microsoft deployed a server-side fix on November 19 to prevent further exploitation and reviewed available telemetry to identify unauthorized API calls affecting customers. The company finished its investigation on November 20 and began notifying affected organizations. Microsoft has not disclosed how many organizations were impacted, but more than a dozen administrators have reported receiving the notification in the Reddit post. Some managed service providers (MSPs) also reported receiving notifications for multiple customer tenants, with one administrator saying the emails arrived hours apart. The notification says no software updates or other customer remediation are required to address the vulnerability. However, Microsoft recommends that organizations alert their security teams to potential targeted phishing and social-engineering attacks that could target the exposed administrator email addresses and tenant information. Organizations are also advised to ensure privileged accounts use phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, review their Connect Health configurations, and examine Microsoft Entra audit and sign-in logs for suspicious activity. Microsoft also published a PowerShell script at https://aka.ms/ConnectHealth/scripts that allows administrators to view the types of tenant metadata that could have been exposed. However, the script displays current configuration values rather than the information that was accessed during the breach. Microsoft has not disclosed who exploited the vulnerability, how many tenants were impacted, or when the attacks first began. When contacted by BleepingComputer, Microsoft confirmed that it had fixed the vulnerability and notified impacted customers. "We identified and addressed a security issue affecting Microsoft Entra Connect Health that could have resulted in unauthorized access to tenant-level contact and configuration metadata. We deployed a fix on November 19, 2026, and have notified impacted customers through Azure Service Health, providing guidance and support," a Microsoft spokesperson told BleepingComputer. Microsoft declined to provide further details about the breach. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. The exposed data included technical contact emails, tenant IDs, display names, domain details, license tiers, directory sync status, and an expired certificate stored in the API. Fix: Microsoft deployed a server-side fix on November 19, 2026, to prevent further exploitation of the Entra Connect Health API vulnerability.

history.title: FBI reportedly hacked again, this time targeting nationwide police database
history.text: FBI systems have reportedly been breached for the second time in two months, this time targeting the agency's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), which is used to share information between local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies. The National Crime Information Center is an FBI-operated database used by law enforcement agencies across the United States to share information about wanted and missing persons, outstanding arrest warrants, stolen vehicles and firearms, protection orders, and other criminal justice records. Police officers routinely use the system during traffic stops, criminal investigations, and background checks. According to CNN's reporting, the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of the NCIC system, citing two people briefed on the investigation. The intrusion was reportedly discovered in recent days, although it is unclear when the breach occurred, how the attackers gained access, or whether any information was stolen. The FBI has not publicly confirmed the incident and did not respond to CNN's request for comment. The reported breach comes just two months after the ShinyHunters extortion group claimed to have breached the FBI's systems by exploiting an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability. The earlier attack targeted a third-party platform associated with the FBI's recruitment website, FBIJobs.gov, with ShinyHunters claiming to have stolen sensitive information from the agency's systems. The FBI subsequently launched an investigation that led to the arrests of suspected ShinyHunters members, including a Canadian cybersecurity executive reportedly linked to the attacks. There is currently no indication that the latest NCIC incident is connected to ShinyHunters or the earlier breach. It remains unclear whether the attackers accessed sensitive law enforcement records stored in NCIC or whether the intrusion affected the system's availability to law enforcement agencies. BleepingComputer contacted the FBI on Friday evening with questions about the reported breach but has not received a response. The intrusion was discovered recently, but officials have not determined when it occurred, how attackers gained access, or whether any data was stolen. This comes two months after a separate incident involving the ShinyHunters group, which exploited an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability and targeted a third-party platform linked to FBIJobs.gov.

history.title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
history.text: The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed. The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands. “Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.” But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company]. The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors. The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260. The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260. Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data. Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.” The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.” “Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed. Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network. A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked. But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days. “The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.” Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further. In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit. “The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.” The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf. “I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.” Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256. “If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.” The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky, an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million. In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.
history.summary: The CTO and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, was indicted for wire fraud after an FBI sting operation revealed the company paid ransomware groups for decryption keys while charging victims a markup for work never performed. Palacio secretly contacted a fictitious ransomware group controlled by the FBI and charged the fake victim $16,010—including a $2,750 diagnostic fee and $13,260 for decryption—while the actual cost to the company was around $6,000 in bitcoin. The company had claimed to use advanced cryptographic tools and a 99% success rate to restore 100% of data, but investigations found it made farcical technical claims and targeted unsuspecting small to medium-sized businesses.

history.title: Attackers' AI Agents Found a Zero-Day in Medical-Imaging Software and Gained Root Access
history.text: Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server, and gain root access to a university server, Amazon Threat Intelligence said this week. The flaw allows an attacker with no account to write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup, which runs with no login enabled. The maintainers have merged a fix in the source code, but there is still no fixed version to install. MONAI Label is a server that research teams use to label medical scans and train imaging models; it is a separate program from the broader MONAI framework. The weakness is a path-traversal flaw in the parts of the server that store uploaded images and labels. A file identifier supplied by the caller is appended to the storage folder and written to disk without checking that the result remains within that folder. The server writes with the privileges of the account it runs under, so an attacker cannot write anywhere on the machine, but a writable code or settings location can open a path to running code. Authentication is off by default, so any client that can reach the server over the network can set off the write. Versions 0.8.5 and earlier are affected. Amazon reconstructed the intrusion after finding the operator's own Cairn control panel sitting on the internet without a password. Cairn is an open-source framework that runs AI agents as automated penetration testers, and the exposed panel revealed the agents' task settings, prompts, and run history. Over about 48 hours in September, the agents mapped the application's interface and reached the point of writing files to the server in roughly 11 minutes, the company said in its incident report. The agents worked with little step-by-step direction. The operator set the goal of getting shell access and chose the targets, and the agents selected the methods themselves, according to the company. Investigators tie the campaign to a China-linked actor with moderate confidence, pointing to Simplified Chinese prompts, China Standard Time settings, and targets likely of interest to China. They did not connect the work to a named group or establish that a government was behind it. A root shell came later, and not within those 11 minutes. In a separate session, the agents used the same flaw to plant a file that Python runs automatically at startup. They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root. That root access was on one university server, and whether another MONAI Label system would give the same result depends on how it is run and what its service account can do. In a later session, the operator handed the agents a tunnel into a second university network running the same software. Amazon believes the network was broken into in the same way but has not confirmed the second compromise. The maintainers confirmed the flaw and merged the source fix on October 19, which forces uploads to resolve inside the approved folders and rejects empty names or names that begin with a dot. Their security advisory, published earlier this week, still lists no patched version and says the correction will arrive in a future release. The newest release listing remains 0.8.5, which dates to 2024. A merged fix in source code is not the same as a package you can install. The flaw is now listed in the CVE record as CVE-2026-133968, published this week and rated 9.8 out of 10, a critical score. The project's advisory still shows no CVE assigned, which is a lag in updating that page, not a sign of a second flaw. What to Do Now With no fixed release available, the practical steps are to cut off exposure and limit what a compromised server could reach: - Block untrusted network access to MONAI Label servers with firewall and routing rules, not just hard-to-guess URLs. - Turn on authentication, which the server leaves off by default. - Run the server under a limited account rather than root, and restrict the folders it can write to. - Do not assume a source build is safe. Confirm it includes the October fix before treating it as patched. - If a server was reachable, check for unexpected Python startup files and unusual training jobs, the path the reported attack used. The company's account is based on its own reconstruction and has not been independently confirmed. It does not show that patient scans or records were taken, that clinical systems were touched, or that the attacker reached past the university targets described. The campaign also included failed operations, and the root result on one server should not be taken as the outcome for every MONAI Label deployment.
history.summary: Autonomous AI agents linked to China‑based actors exploited a path‑traversal flaw in MONAI Label, an open‑source medical‑imaging server, to gain root access on university systems. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE‑2026‑133968, allows unauthenticated attackers to write files outside the intended storage folder by manipulating a file identifier. Maintainers have merged a source‑code fix that restricts uploads to approved folders and rejects empty or dot‑prefixed names, but no patched package is currently available for installation.

history.title: BADBOX botnet returns with record-breaking 40 billion daily ad requests
history.text: The BADBOX malware botnet has returned following last year's disruptions, generating a record 40 billion fraudulent advertising bid requests per day through infected Android-based devices. According to HUMAN's Satori researchers, who uncovered and disrupted the latest variant, BADBOX 3.0 had grown into the largest documented ad-fraud operation by daily bid request volume. BADBOX was first discovered in early 2023 on a T95 Android TV box bought on Amazon. In December 2024, Germany's cybersecurity agencies warned that the botnet had infected tens of thousands of devices. In March 2025, a large-scale disruption operation took place where HUMAN and Shadowserver cut off more than 500,000 BADBOX 2.0 devices from their control servers, while Google removed 24 apps that spread the malware from Google Play. Google later sued the botnet's operators, saying the BADBOX 2.0 had infected over 10 million Android-based devices by April 2025. BadBox returns However, the previous disruptions didn't stop the BADBOX operators from rebuilding the botnet and setting new records for daily fraudulent advertising bid requests. "At its height, BADBOX 3.0 accounted for roughly 40 billion bid requests a day and more than 4% of all CTV traffic observed by the Human Defense Platform," reports HUMAN. "BADBOX 3.0's volume was more than three times the volume of the previous record holder, VASTFLUX, and represents a larger peak than the last five years' worth of published Satori investigations combined." The modus operandi remains the same: infecting cheap phones, tablets, and streaming TV boxes running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP) with malware that performs ad fraud and traffic proxying. The malware performs ad fraud by playing video ads in hidden windows while impersonating legitimate streaming apps to make the requests appear legitimate. HUMAN also observed fraudulent server-side ad insertion (SSAI) requests that tricked advertisers into believing ads were played on streaming devices, even though no actual device or video ad was involved. A proxying module also enrolled infected devices in one of 11 residential proxy networks without the owners' knowledge or consent. One of those networks, PXYEDGE, was identified as the rebranded successor to IpMoYu, a residential proxy service previously linked to BADBOX 2.0. The researchers say PXYEDGE advertised approximately 200,000 proxy nodes, while their monitoring showed unique connections peaking at around 340,000. HUMAN says some of the ad fraud traffic was also routed through these residential proxies to appear legitimate and evade anti-abuse filters. The researchers linked the malware to a specific Chinese electronics manufacturer through its domains, device-specific checks in the code, a factory-installed TV launcher, and a repository maintainer. The infected devices fetch malware modules from public code repositories, while the same payloads are also mirrored across various hosting platforms for redundancy and to resist takedowns. HUMAN says it also participated in Google's disruption of the related XCPE malware operation earlier this month, which included taking down multiple C2 domains used by BADBOX 3.0. Additionally, one of the malware repositories was taken down, while HUMAN says its systems now filter fraudulent advertising traffic associated with BADBOX 3.0. However, HUMAN warns that the botnet operators are likely to adapt to the latest disruption, as they have done in the past. Users should only buy certified Android devices from reputable manufacturers and ensure that Play Protect is available and active. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. history.title: Amazon: China-Linked Hackers’ AI Agents Exploited Medical Software Zero-Day
history.text: Amazon says autonomous AI agents run by a China-linked threat actor found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open source tool designed for AI-assisted annotation of medical images. The tech giant’s threat intelligence team detected the activity in September, after coming across an exposed instance of Cairn, an open source AI penetration testing framework. The instance had no authentication, so anyone could see the operator’s prompts and the agents’ output. The records showed a roughly 48-hour campaign against IP addresses belonging to universities in East Asia outside mainland China. The operator gave the agents a list of targets and told them to obtain shell access. After identifying the software on one target and mapping its API, the agents discovered a path traversal bug in a file upload function. “In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server,” Amazon said. In a later session, the agents used the flaw to plant a Python reverse shell in a file Python runs every time the interpreter starts, ultimately achieving a root shell. “Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, issue, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project,” the company said. The operator then gave the agents a proxy that tunneled into a second university and instructed them to target other devices on its network. “The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon noted. The MONAI Label developers published an advisory this week. It rates the bug critical and says it affects versions 0.8.5 and earlier. Authentication is off by default, enabling anyone who can reach the server over the network to exploit the vulnerability. A fix has been created and will be included in the next release. Amazon has attributed the attack to an unidentified Chinese-nexus threat actor with moderate confidence, based on the language used in the prompts, the time zone in the scripts, and the fact that the targeted universities are likely of strategic interest to China. Related: European Commission Confirms AI-Assisted Cyberattack Disrupted Services Related: China-Linked Hackers Exploit PHP2Shell to Root Firewalls Related: Barracuda Hacked Amid Surge in Artex-Powered Cyberattacks
history.summary: Amazon's threat intelligence team discovered that China-linked actors used autonomous AI agents to exploit a zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, an open-source medical AI annotation tool. The agents mapped the application's API, arbitrarily wrote files to the server, and planted a Python reverse shell to achieve root access within about 11 minutes, targeting university networks in East Asia via an exposed, unauthenticated Cairn penetration testing framework. Amazon assesses with high confidence that the flaw was a zero-day, and the MONAI Label developers have since published a critical advisory affecting versions 0.8.5 and earlier, noting that authentication is off by default and a fix has been created for the next release.

history.title: A Single Malicious Webpage Let Researchers Hijack Meta Muse and Access Private Chats
history.text: A malicious webpage could extract a Meta Muse user's private conversations and stored memories from the assistant without triggering any approval prompt, researchers have shown. The same attack could be extended to reach the credentials Muse stores for the user's connected accounts. The work was a laboratory demonstration, not an attack on real users, and it stayed inside the individual user's cloud machine. NebuSec, the security firm that published it yesterday, says Muse's team has since fixed every weakness it describes. Muse is Meta's personal AI agent, launched on September 8, that works through the online accounts a user connects to it and can make purchases on their behalf. Each person's agent runs on its own cloud computer. There, a monitoring layer called Sentinel is meant to be the single gate for anything the agent sends out, and the passwords and tokens for connected accounts are supposed to stay beyond the agent's reach. Muse's team described the aim at launch: "So we designed the system to assume the agent may be under attack and limit the potential damage." In the demonstration, a malicious page the agent opened could pull a user's conversation history and stored memories to an external server and alter them, with no prompt shown to the user, according to the firm's research write-up. From there, the researchers chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser, which the assistant uses for tasks such as creating PDFs, to a Linux kernel flaw, thereby taking full control of the user's cloud machine. They set out that chain in a technical breakdown. That full control reached the credential store, the saved files, and Sentinel itself, the parts Muse's security design keeps walled off from the agent. The compromise went no further than that one machine. The researchers did not break out to the shared server beneath it or into other users' machines. Muse was built to assume its own agent could be turned against the user and to box in any break-in. Each of those controls worked as designed, the firm said, yet the attack still ran the whole way through. The firm says it reported the findings to Muse's team and that the exploits were all fixed before publication. Meta has not publicly confirmed the fixes or commented on the work, and the write-up does not say whether any user data was accessed before the patches went in. The firm's Muse research broke into the cloud system behind the assistant, unlike an earlier Muse flaw found in September, which only let malware already on a user's Mac hijack the assistant on the device.
history.summary: A malicious webpage could extract Muse users' private conversations and stored memories without triggering any approval prompt, researchers showed. The attack chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser with a Linux kernel flaw to gain full control of the user's cloud machine, reaching credentials, saved files, and the Sentinel monitoring layer. NebuSec reported the findings, and Muse's team fixed all described weaknesses before publication, though Meta has not publicly confirmed the fixes.

history.title: GnuPG Warns Critical GPGME Flaw Could Expose App Data via Malicious OpenPGP Keys
history.text: A malicious OpenPGP key with an unusually long user ID can trigger a critical memory bug in GPGME, the standard library that programs use to work with GnuPG. The GnuPG project warned yesterday that the flaw could be used to steal data from affected applications and has released fixed versions. The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-129975, affects all software that uses GPGME before version 2.3.0, whether the library is loaded as a shared library, a Windows DLL, or statically linked into the program. Examples the project gives include most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba, and its own Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, and GnuPG VS-Desktop packages. The project has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, and it notes that remote code execution cannot be ruled out. Its example of a path to the bug is signed data sent to an application. Which programs pass such material to the library without a manual key import is not something the advisory says. The flaw is a double free, meaning the same memory is released twice. It sits in two routines, read_status() and read_colon_line(), that read status lines and key listings coming back from GnuPG. When the input runs long, the routines move the data to a larger buffer but record the new address only if they finish without errors. An error in between leaves a pointer to memory that was already freed, and cleanup then frees it a second time, as the project's tracker entry details. The flaw was found by Johan Carlsson and reported to the project by GitLab last week. Disclosure was set for November 25, the advisory says, and moved up because the new Ruby2Shell bug forced the company to update earlier. What to Update The fixed library version is GPGME 2.3.1, released this week. A version 2.3.0 was never publicly available. What to install depends on where the library sits: - Shared library or DLL: update to GPGME 2.3.1, available from the project's official downloads and detailed in its security advisory. - Windows: Gpg4win 5.1.2 bundles the fixed library. Its release notes call the issue severe and say to update as soon as possible. - Older versions that cannot move to 2.3.1: the advisory carries a patch, and the legacy branch has its own fixed release, 1.24.4, whose legacy release notes say the project cannot guarantee that the branch will see every security patch. - Bundled and statically linked copies: these are affected too, and updates to the system's shared library do not reach them, so the applications that contain them need their own rebuilt releases. - GPGMEPP and GPGMEQT: no update is needed. The advisory offers no interim workaround for software that cannot update yet.
history.summary: GnuPG warned of a critical double-free flaw in GPGME (CVE-2026-129975) triggered by malicious OpenPGP keys with unusually long user IDs, which could expose application data. The bug affects all software using GPGME before version 2.3.0 and resides in `read_status()` and `read_colon_line()`, where input errors leave pointers to already-freed memory, causing a second free. The GnuPG project released fixed versions and related updates to resolve the issue.

history.title: Signal Blocks AI Agents From Reading Private Chats via Screenshots on Android and iOS
history.text: Signal has announced that it will restrict screenshots by default to stop artificial intelligence (AI) agents from reading private chats on Android and iOS devices, but conceded that the protection is "incomplete." The feature applies to agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where the encrypted messaging platform can detect an AI assistant attempting to read the Signal screen. It also builds upon a similar setting that Signal introduced in Windows 11 last May following Microsoft's release of the controversial Recall feature. Calling the agentic integrations into Android, iOS, and Windows an "existential threat to Signal," Meredith Whittaker, president of the Signal Foundation, said the move is designed to uphold its privacy guarantees in the AI era. "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that's on your screen," Whittaker said. "In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." "The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy." The risk here is that AI agents can capture and store the information accessed from Signal either locally or on remote servers, with the activity occurring outside of the platform's control and potentially putting the privacy of all the participants in a conversation at risk. Users who want to disable the option can do so by navigating to Settings > Privacy > App Security > toggle "Block Siri AI" (on iOS) or "Screen security" (on Android). "However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts') Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees," Signal said. "Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user's device via the file system." Signal also pointed out that application developers lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from eroding application-level privacy. It also called out the companies for failing to provide adequate documentation about how these systems work to help design necessary controls to prevent the agents from accessing sensitive application data. Specifically, it's urging the tech giants to provide "two common-sense remedies" to help protect the privacy of its users - - Access to easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing entirely, including screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, without making drastic compromises to the core user experience - Create better documentation and technical specifications around how AI agents function, specifically with regards to data access and processing The concerns are not theoretical. Reuters recently reported that Muse, Meta's AI agent, was able to bypass its own official "Connector" tool to obtain access to Signal messages on both an Apple computer and an Android device by taking advantage of the broad operating system permissions granted to it during initial setup. On macOS, for example, the agent leveraged macOS's accessibility and screenshot tools to navigate to the Signal app, take screenshots, extract text from those images, and regenerate the textual content within the Muse app. On Android, it read messages by abusing its access to the device's push notifications. In one case highlighted by the news agency, the AI agent alerted a Meta staffer using Muse on her personal phone with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal. "This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this," the employee said in an internal post. "We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta's Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup," Whittaker said. "In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents." Late last month, Apple released iOS 27.2 with an "Excluded Apps" option that lets users choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access. With Google Gemini, users have the ability to disconnect apps via the Connected Apps settings. Earlier this week, the iPhone maker also previewed new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

history.title: Cleverbridge warns hackers stole credit card numbers, CVVs in data breach
history.text: E-commerce platform Cleverbridge is warning that hackers breached its systems and stole customers' payment card information, including credit card numbers and CVV security codes. Cleverbridge provides e-commerce services to software and SaaS companies, allowing them to sell products, process payments, and manage subscriptions. The company lists numerous technology brands as its customers, including Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Sony, and Parallels. However, it has not disclosed which businesses' customers were impacted by the breach. In a new page about the security incident, Cleverbridge says it detected unauthorized activity on November 4, 2026, and temporarily took systems offline to contain the breach. "All systems were brought back online on 4 November 2026; however, our investigation subsequently determined that a third party copied payment card data stored on our platform," reads the security incident disclosure. Cleverbridge began notifying affected customers on November 20, warning that hackers had stolen payment card details used to make purchases through its platform. While its public disclosure confirms the theft of payment card data, it does not specify which card details were stolen, instead referring affected customers to their individual notifications for more information. However, a breach notification shared with BleepingComputer reveals that the stolen information includes payment card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV/CVC security codes. "Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes the payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC)," reads the notification. "Note however that no other personal data (for example your name, contact or billing details) were copied. The affected card ends in XXXX." BleepingComputer redacted the last four digits of the affected payment card. The company has not disclosed how the attackers gained access to its platform, how long they remained in its systems, or how many customers were affected by the breach. Of particular concern is the theft of CVV/CVC security codes, which are used to verify payment card transactions. Cleverbridge also confirmed that the incident was not a ransomware attack and that attackers did not encrypt any of its systems. The company says it has notified data protection authorities, law enforcement, payment card networks, and payment partners about the incident. Cleverbridge is also working with TransUnion's Cyberscout to distribute breach notifications and provide affected customers with complimentary credit monitoring and fraud assistance. Affected customers are told to review their payment card statements for unauthorized transactions. Cleverbridge also recommends contacting card issuers about the incident, as banks may decide to replace compromised cards. BleepingComputer contacted Cleverbridge with questions about how many customers were affected, how the attackers accessed its systems, whether the stolen payment card data was encrypted, and why CVV/CVC security codes were accessible. Unauthorized activity was detected on November 4, 2026, and systems were temporarily taken offline to contain the breach before being brought back online the same day. Affected customers were notified starting November 20, and the company confirmed no other personal data was copied; it also stated the incident was not ransomware and has since notified authorities, law enforcement, and payment networks while offering credit monitoring through TransUnion's Cyberscout.

history.title: OpenRouter Drops 3 Providers After Researchers Catch Months of Prompt Theft at AI Hosting Firms
history.text: Attackers stole data from inside three AI inference providers for months, and none of the three knew until researchers told them, the industrial cybersecurity company Dragos said this week. Some of the stolen requests were flagged as Zero Data Retention, the setting that is supposed to mean a prompt is never stored. OpenRouter, a gateway that routes customers' AI requests to a pool of third-party providers, said today that it has removed three providers from its platform, removed 125 endpoints from eligibility for Zero Data Retention, and notified all potentially affected customers. The findings showed no breach of OpenRouter itself, the company said. The earliest of the three breaches began in mid-July. The planted prompts were bait, but they were processed alongside real customer requests, and those were almost certainly copied too, the firm said. The finding comes from canary token research that seeded about two million prompts with unique web links and credentials between July and November, then watched for anyone using them. A planted secret can only be learned in one place, so any use of it means someone read the prompt that carried it. The largest of the three breaches involved a couple hundred AWS keys that were planted, each sent in exactly one request to one provider during a few short windows in late October. Every request sent during those windows was stolen, and some came from requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, indicating the attacker was copying traffic at the first point of arrival rather than deeper in the inference stack. The thief tested keys within hours in some cases, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users to keep access, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls. One attacker appears to have compromised two of the providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server. On November 1, the same attacker brought in ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration testing framework, and used it only to confirm that keys it already held were still live. Two of its user agents, artex-agent and artex-judge-r121, appear in no public indicator list the firm could find and are worth adding to detections. "A privacy flag doesn't help when the attacker is already inside," wrote HD Moore, the firm's chief research officer. The second finding needed no break-in. Sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest prices, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through, the research found. The people doing it looked like individuals on home internet connections. One, working from a Mac on home broadband in France, took passwords from two prompts and typed root SSH login attempts by hand, then used the same machine to test several planted AWS keys. One of those keys had traveled through a different router that quietly forwarded some of its traffic to the marketplace, a hop that no customer was told about. That router has since told the firm it stopped, and route tracing across about 2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems, plus one seller that quietly adds about 1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt. A Chinese AI lab, which the research does not name, fetched the secret links from more than half of the seeded prompts sent to its models between July and October, including about two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention. Prompts sent to U.S. hosting providers that resell the lab's models triggered the same scraper, thereby flowing back to the lab. A git client on another cloud later tried to clone private repositories referenced in the prompts, but only for that lab's models, and one large U.S. provider kept crawling a secret link more than two months after a single request to its search endpoint. Twenty-four days after one prompt was sent, its secret link was posted into a chat on Feishu, the Chinese workplace app known as Lark elsewhere. The link was opened within two minutes from three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai. The firm had disclosed only the first 8 characters of the provider's link, so whoever posted it was reading a cached copy of the full prompt. In practice, Moore wrote, the flagged prompts were kept, passed to other companies, and read by human beings. OpenRouter said in an incident announcement that the 125 endpoints removed from Zero Data Retention eligibility cover providers flagged by the researchers plus others cut as a precaution. Any endpoint removed during the review will require assurances and validation before its status is returned. The gateway is adapting the researchers' testing approach so that the checks can run on an ongoing basis and is verifying network paths to identify where requests and responses may be forwarded to third parties. The researchers are now working with about a dozen providers, and planted keys and secret links were still being accessed months after the first thefts, as of this week. Railway, a platform company, said in October that an intrusion it suffered was likely part of a series of attacks built to target platform companies with the end goal of compromising AI inference providers. Not all affected providers have posted publicly, the gateway said, and it has notified affected users either way. Three have posted. What the Providers Have Disclosed An attacker took control of an inference server at Phala and could view request data while it was being processed, the provider said in a preliminary incident report last week. The incident was contained on November 8, and the model service has been restored with added protections. Requests to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model that reached Phala through the gateway between October 21 at 00:00 UTC and November 8 at 05:35 UTC should be treated as exposed, the report says, and every key, token, password, or other secret within them should be rotated. A third-party researcher had been placing unique canary credentials in requests since July 1, and only the ones sent on October 21 and 22 were later misused. Those tests sampled traffic rather than monitoring every request, so the provider maintains the broader precautionary window. At Together AI, an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples of customer prompts after an AI coding agent committed a credential to the company's public GitHub repository, the company said yesterday in a security notice. The samples had been collected for routine software testing and were generated by requests to the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models in June and July. The party searched the samples for credentials to other services and tested them, and five of the tested credentials were canaries from the researchers' experiment. The company said it has no reason to believe the data went further, understands it has been deleted, and has made zero data retention the default for new accounts. Novita, another provider on the gateway, confirmed this week in a privacy notice that a routing configuration issue caused some MiniMax requests to be sent on to MiniMax's official API, beyond what was intended for those customers. Dragos has not named the three breached providers, OpenRouter has not named the three it removed, and neither has said publicly whether they are the same three. The provider behind the mid-July breach first blamed an internal misconfiguration, then a partner's data processing, before its own investigation found that attackers had compromised its internal credentials, the researchers said. It had still not disclosed the incident publicly as of this week. What Users Should Do The researchers' advice starts from one limit: a privacy flag binds only the first hop, Moore wrote, and AI agents will send whatever they can read, credentials included. Where a prompt goes is a choice, he wrote, and a customer who does not choose hands the choice to the lowest price. Self-hosting is the only option in which no third party reads a prompt, and going directly to a first-tier provider leaves one company, one contract, and one privacy policy to check. Routers need more care: pick the upstream providers yourself instead of accepting the default pool, verify that privacy settings actually change where requests go, and stay away from reseller marketplaces, some of whose capacity runs on stolen keys. A fake credential seeded into the context that agents and pipelines already send serves as a tripwire if any use of it is treated as an incident, and a free Thinkst Canarytoken is enough to get started. Settings that scrub known credential formats from prompts help too, though they miss sensitive data that is not shaped like a key.
history.summary: OpenRouter removed three providers and 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility after researchers found attackers stole data from AI inference providers for months by embedding canary tokens in prompts, with the earliest breach starting in mid-July and the largest involving hundreds of AWS keys extracted from traffic at the first point of arrival. A separate issue involved marketplace sellers and resellers quietly logging and forwarding prompts, including one that added hidden tokens to every request and another that routed traffic through unidentified systems, while a Chinese AI lab accessed secret links from over half of Zero Data Retention prompts, causing them to flow back to U.S. resellers.

history.title: FBI Investigating Apparent Hack of Its Key National Criminal Justice Database, AP Source Says
history.text: The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database that it maintains, a person familiar with the matter said Saturday. The National Crime Information Center, known as the NCIC, is a computerized database of criminal justice information that is available to local, state and federal law enforcement agencies and includes records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history data, stolen property and other topics. The FBI declined to comment Saturday on the apparent hack, which was first reported by CNN and confirmed to The Associated Press by a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak by name and spoke on the condition of anonymity. The scope of the problem was not immediately clear. Asked about the subject on Saturday, President Donald Trump said in a Fox News Channel interview: “We just heard about it, and I will say that it’s not good.” News that the NCIC was targeted comes as the country has encountered a series of digital outages in the government and private sector that Trump administration officials have said were caused by routine efforts to upgrade computer systems and fix vulnerabilities, rather than a cyberattack. There was no immediate indication that the FBI incident was related to those outages. The bureau has historically been a frequent target for hackers. In September, for instance, a criminal hacking group known as ShinyHunters revealed that it had obtained a massive trove of data on FBI employees and applicants and had compromised the bureau’s jobs portal. And in March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating “suspicious activities” on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. Related: Ransomware Response Expert Arrested in ShinyHunters FBI Hack Probe Related: ShinyHunters Claims FBI Hack, Demands Retraction of Threat Report
history.summary: FBI is investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database. The NCIC is a computerized database of criminal justice information accessible to law enforcement, containing records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history, and stolen property. The scope of the problem is not yet clear, and President Trump commented that it "is not good," while administration officials have attributed other recent digital outages to routine system upgrades rather than cyberattacks, with no immediate indication the NCIC incident is related.

history.title: Rackspace Spot breach let hackers access customer Kubernetes secrets
history.text: Rackspace warned customers that hackers breached its Rackspace Spot cloud platform using compromised credentials, allowing them to deploy unauthorized workloads and access Kubernetes secrets in customer clusters. Rackspace Spot is a cloud platform that allows organizations to deploy and manage containerized applications using Kubernetes. The company disclosed the breach in a notification sent to affected customers and obtained by BleepingComputer, stating that attackers accessed parts of the platform on November 17, 2026, between approximately 00:20 and 22:00 UTC. Rackspace says it learned of the intrusion on November 18 after receiving a customer report and confirmed that the recipient's organization was affected that same day. "On 17 November 2026 (about 00:20–22:00 UTC), an unauthorized party used leaked credentials to access parts of Rackspace Spot," reads the notification. According to Rackspace, the attackers were able to act as legitimate users in some customer organizations, allowing them to create pods in Kubernetes clusters, read Kubernetes Secrets, and list nodes and volumes. Kubernetes Secrets store sensitive information such as passwords, authentication tokens, and API keys that can be used to access databases, cloud services, and other systems. Rackspace warned that the attackers could have read any Secret stored in an affected user's clusters, as well as any Spot API tokens or refresh tokens held by that user. The company says it has since revoked affected tokens and sessions, removed the unauthorized pods, rotated keys, and strengthened access controls and monitoring. Affected customers have been instructed to reissue their Spot API tokens, replace refresh tokens used in automation tools, download fresh Kubernetes configuration files, and rotate credentials stored in their cluster Secrets. Rackspace also advised customers to analyze logs associated with databases, container registries, Git repositories, cloud storage, and third-party services dating back to November 17 to identify possible abuse of exposed credentials. The company shared the following indicators of compromise associated with the attack: - IP address: 23.224.79.106 - IP range: 23.224.0.0/15 - Suspicious Kubernetes pod and object prefixes: i1, glm-, and probe BleepingComputer contacted Rackspace to ask how many customers were affected and whether customer data was stolen, but has not received a response. The breach also caused an extended outage of the Rackspace Spot administration console, temporarily preventing customers from managing their clusters and rotating potentially compromised credentials. In a Reddit discussion, Sirish Raghuram, co-founder and Chief Growth Officer of Platform9, which co-developed Rackspace Spot with Rackspace, explained that the company deliberately disabled access while securing its infrastructure. "I've been instrumental in creating Spot and in its operations to date, and I can tell you that the team and I are incredibly disappointed to have let you down in this way," Raghuram said. "I know you disagree, but we made the decision that shutting all access down and sanitizing the entire environment is what we can do to best protect everyone using Spot." After multiple delays, Rackspace announced that service had been fully restored on November 21. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. Attackers acted as legitimate users, creating pods, reading Kubernetes Secrets containing passwords and tokens, and listing nodes and volumes, with Rackspace confirming the intrusion the next day after a customer report.

history.title: Researchers Demonstrate Ghostscript Sandbox-Escape RCE via Crafted File Uploads in Popular Apps
history.text: A now-patched flaw in Ghostscript allows a crafted file to escape the program's security sandbox and run commands on the server that processes it. Ghostscript is the interpreter that many Linux servers use to convert uploaded PDFs, PostScript files, and images into other formats, often without the application calling it directly. Security firm pwn.ai showed this week that ordinary upload, preview, and print features in about ten common applications could be tricked into feeding it such a file. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125396, was fixed on September 8, and there have been no reports of it being used in attacks. Getting a crafted file to Ghostscript is easy, because an application does not have to call it directly. A common image or document library such as ImageMagick, Pillow, libvips, or a Qt plugin will hand PostScript or EPS content to Ghostscript to render, even when the file is named .png, .jpg, or .pdf. A routine feature like making a thumbnail or cropping a picture can start the interpreter, and the exact path depends on the libraries the application uses. The underlying bug is a use-after-free in the part of Ghostscript that loads fonts. A crafted document uses it to switch off the checks in -dSAFER, the sandbox that is supposed to stop the document from running commands or reaching files. The security firm demonstrated the result by feeding such a document through about ten applications and watching a command run on the server, each time as the low-privilege account that does the rendering. Several of those paths needed no login: an anonymous print job to a shared Debian 13 queue, an emailed attachment that Roundcube webmail processed the moment the recipient opened the message, and public upload forms in the WordPress plugins Forminator and Essential Addons for Elementor. WordPress Core itself needed more: an account with the ability to upload files, which Authors and higher roles have by default. Although the CVE is classified as a local flaw, the firm's tests reached Ghostscript from the network via print jobs, email, and web uploads. The tested version and the access needed for each application are set out in its impact index. Artifex, which develops Ghostscript, fixed the flaw in version 10.08.0 on September 8, and is moving the vulnerable internal step into safer code. Ken Sharp, the developer who handled the fix, called that step "an ancient piece of code well known to be a vulnerability, but difficult to eradicate" in the bug report. The CVE was published last week and is scored 8.5 out of 10 in its security advisory. WordPress had already closed its own upload path in version 7.0.4 on August 12, under a separate identifier, CVE-2026-65640, as noted in its release notes. That fix and the Ghostscript fix cover different points in the same chain, so updating one does not remove the need for the other. Updating the Renderer The fix helps only where it reaches the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not update a separate copy of Ghostscript bundled inside a container image or an application, so a document worker can keep running the old code after the host package is replaced. Coverage across Linux distributions is uneven. As of last week, several still shipped a vulnerable Ghostscript or had a fix pending, according to the firm's survey. The list records package status, not a tested attack path for each system: - Debian 12 (Bookworm): listed as vulnerable - Amazon Linux 2, 2023, and 2027 Preview: fix pending - SUSE Linux Enterprise 12 SP5 and parts of 15: fix in progress - SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 and 16.1: fix in progress - openSUSE Leap 16.0 and 16.1: affected The firm did not establish whether current Red Hat, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, or stable Fedora packages carry the fix. Until the renderer is updated, the exposure can be reduced by requiring authentication on print queues and by limiting which file types an image processor accepts. System controls help too, and in one test an AppArmor profile stopped the compromised interpreter from starting a shell. One published proof-of-concept file, described in its technical analysis, shows only the core memory trick. It changes a value inside the running interpreter and sets it back, without running a shell command or touching files on the host, and on the patched 10.08.0 build it fails before that point. The firm's broader research extended to production services, including Google, which fixed the affected path last week. Its reports of similar problems at Dropbox and other unnamed services are separate Ghostscript bugs, not this one.
history.summary: A patched flaw in Ghostscript (CVE-2026-125396) allows a crafted file to escape its security sandbox and run commands on the server, affecting many applications that process PDFs, PostScript, or images without directly calling Ghostscript. Security firm pwn.ai demonstrated the exploit through about ten common apps, including print jobs, email attachments, and WordPress plugins, reaching the interpreter as a low-privilege rendering account, with the bug being a use-after-free in font loading that disables -dSAFER checks. Fix: The flaw was fixed in Ghostscript 10.08.0 on September 8, and WordPress already closed its related upload path in version 7.0.4 under CVE-2026-65640, though both fixes are needed as they cover different points in the same chain.

history.title: Hackers exploit GL.iNet cloud flaw to infect routers, KVM devices
history.text: GL.iNet has confirmed that hackers exploited a vulnerability in its cloud remote management services to install custom malware on customers' routers and KVM devices, with some affected users reporting backdoors and reverse shells giving remote access to infected devices. GL.iNet manufactures networking equipment, including home and travel routers, as well as KVM devices that allow users to access and control computers remotely. Its GoodCloud platform allows customers to remotely manage supported devices, including accessing and controlling computers and servers connected to its KVM products. In a security advisory published on November 20, GL.iNet confirmed that an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in its cloud remote management services to access devices and install malicious software. "The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident," the company said. "Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. These measures do not remove malware from devices that were already infected." GL.iNet has not disclosed how the attackers exploited its cloud platform, how many customers were impacted, or whether information was stolen from compromised devices. The company is also investigating whether computers connected to infected KVM devices were compromised. GL.iNet recommends that customers check their devices for signs of infection and install the latest security firmware, even if no malware is detected. The company's initial instructions told customers to look for a process running as crond -i /tmp/.log, which GL.iNet said was an indicator of compromise. While the cloud vulnerability has been fixed, GL.iNet says stable firmware updates containing additional security fixes for both routers and KVM devices are scheduled for release on November 22, 2026. For KVM devices, customers can follow the company's firmware upgrade guidance, which recommends version 1.10.3 or later for the RM10, RM1, RM1V2, RM1PE, and RM4PE, version 1.10.3 beta or later for the RM10RC, and version 1.8.7 or later for the RMQ1. Router owners should install the latest security firmware for their specific model as soon as it becomes available. However, GL.iNet forum members warn that the company's detection instructions may not identify all compromised devices, including those infected with other backdoors or running reverse shells. GL.iNet has linked to a community-developed detection and cleanup tool as part of the company's official support instructions for routers and KVM devices. The scanner performs additional checks for known malware files, suspicious processes, modified system utilities, and configuration files modified for persistence. It can also collect forensic evidence and optionally remove known malware components. The project's developers warn that the scanner cannot detect every infection and that compromised devices may require reinstalling firmware without retaining existing settings, as malicious files stored in configuration directories could survive an ordinary firmware upgrade. Customers who suspect their devices were compromised should preserve evidence before resetting them, avoid restoring potentially infected configurations, and rotate credentials and access keys that may have been exposed. GL.iNet also asked customers who run the scanner to upload the anonymous report when prompted so the developers can determine the number and types of devices impacted. For KVM users, the malware may have allowed access to the computers controlled by the KVM, so those devices should also be analyzed for potential compromise. Malware and reverse shells discovered Following the disclosure, GL.iNet customers and security researchers shared evidence of custom malware infections designed specifically for GL.iNET devices, as well as root-level reverse shells that connected compromised routers to the IP address 170.39.226[.]219. The reverse shells used the Linux nc utility to create outbound connections, allowing remote attackers to execute commands on infected devices. Researchers at RemoteToHome Consulting also identified a potential command injection vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud client involving a handler used for AstroWarp/SD-WAN functionality. According to the researchers, the handler passes cloud-supplied values into shell commands executed with root privileges without properly validating them. However, GL.iNet has not confirmed that this particular vulnerability was used in the attacks. RemoteToHome says it analyzed 183 routers it owns or manages and found suspicious activity on 152, including 24 with root-level reverse shells, 47 with an older persistent backdoor, and 81 showing evidence that attacker-supplied commands had executed. The researchers note that their findings may not be the same as the other GL.iNet customers and that the older backdoor infections may not be linked to the November attacks. In a separate forum report, the owner of a compromised GL-RM1 KVM shared network logs showing it downloading a malicious ni.sh script and additional executable payloads from 66.245.219[.]252 on November 19. The owner also reported that the device began communicating with approximately 1,800 residential IP addresses daily and repeatedly contacted the TRON blockchain API, exhibiting activity suggestive of a peer-to-peer network. However, the purpose of these connections is unclear, and there is no confirmation that the compromised devices were being used as residential proxies or were part of a larger botnet. BleepingComputer examined a copy of the malicious ni.sh script [VirusTotal] and found that it contains code specifically tailored to GL.iNet routers and KVM devices. The script recognizes numerous GL.iNet device models and downloads malicious executables named gl-helper and gb from hardcoded servers. It also establishes persistence through startup scripts and scheduled tasks, allowing the malware to restart after a reboot or if its processes are terminated. The installer includes functionality to disguise the malicious process as crond -i /tmp/.log, matching the IOC published by GL.iNet. An interesting feature is replacing the legitimate netstat utility with a modified shell script that filters out connections to 66.245.219[.]252, potentially hiding the malware's communications from administrators examining network connections. The installer also contains functionality to install SSH public keys for remote access, modify file timestamps, and periodically contact a remote server to retrieve and execute commands. The attacker's infrastructure includes two IP addresses, 66.245.219[.]252 and 65.20.71[.]131, which match the IP addresses seen in the compromised KVM owner's logs. The script also contains Chinese-language developer comments describing its persistence mechanisms, reporting functionality, and interactions with GL.iNet's cloud management software, indicating a Chinese-speaking individual may have written it. BleepingComputer also examined a separate malicious Lua payload recovered from a GL-MT2500 router. The payload was launched through a modified urandom_seed startup script and included functionality to collect device information, contact remote servers, and download and execute additional programs. Some of the malicious files recovered from GL.iNet devices had timestamps dating to December 2025, suggesting that some devices may have been compromised for months. However, it is unclear whether these infections involved the same threat actors or were related to the November 20 attacks. GL.iNet says it continues to investigate the incident and plans to notify identified affected customers using the email addresses associated with their cloud accounts.
