history.summary: Stolen credentials exposed customer data at Todoist, where an attacker used a compromised version-control credential to access source code, employee accounts, and cloud infrastructure, affecting 6% of users. A new ransomware group called BYOD disrupted at least nine organizations in October–November 2026, causing ambulance diversions, clinic closures, and device shutdowns through credential compromise and a remote access trojan. More than 10 million exposed NGINX services running HTTP/2 are vulnerable to NGINX2Root, allowing remote unauthenticated attackers to corrupt memory and achieve code execution when ASLR is disabled or bypassed. Fix: Customers should update NGINX to a patched version and disable HTTP/2 or restrict access until a fix is applied.

history.title: FIFA Says It Has Been Victim of a Cyberattack Accessing ‘Personal and Business Information’
history.text: FIFA was the victim of a cyberattack that saw hackers gain access to what soccer’s world governing body describes as a “limited set of personal and business information,” it said Thursday. “FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement,” the organization said in a statement sent to The Associated Press. FIFA didn’t say when the cyberattack took place, or the precise nature of the hacked information. Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot on X of what it claimed were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the hack when responding to a post that said more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been leaked. “FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data,” the governing body said in its statement. “Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.” The breach comes at a time when FIFA and its president, Gianni Infantino, is under scrutiny after his foiled, secretive plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. Infantino is also trying to extend his 11-year presidency of FIFA to 2031. He is the favorite when the election is held on March 18, with Kohzo Tashima of Japan and Philippe Diallo of France the other candidates. Related: 1Password Breach Exposes Customer Data, Internal Source Code Related: US Treasury’s FinCEN Disconnects Systems Following Cyber Incident Related: Plagiarism Checker Turnitin Investigating Cyberattack
history.summary: FIFA confirmed it was victim of a cyberattack resulting in unauthorized access to a limited set of personal and business information. FIFA stated it is working with relevant authorities and law enforcement in response to the incident. A hacking group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club claimed responsibility by posting files on social media and later taking credit for leaking over 12 gigabytes of internal documents.

history.title: North Korea-Linked PolinRider Poisons Over 7,600 GitHub Repositories to Spread Malware
history.text: The threat actors behind the PolinRider campaign have been observed planting a Python loader in GitHub repositories, as evidence emerges that the activity may have started as far back as February 2025. "The loader hides in a small utils package or in conftest.py," SafeDep said in a report published this week. "When Python imports the file, the loader reads the newest transaction that an Ethereum wallet sent to itself. It decodes the input data of that transaction as JavaScript and runs it with Node.js." The JavaScript code, for its part, reads a second wallet to locate the command-and-control (C2) server and then passes the next stage to a detached interactive Node.js environment by means of a node -i process. The software supply chain security company said it identified the loader in 375 public repositories that belong to 260 accounts. There is no evidence that the loader has been distributed via PyPI or npm. PolinRider is the name assigned to a malicious campaign linked to North Korean threat actors. Recent reports indicate that the activity employs various channels to distribute malware, including - - Fraudulent recruitment campaigns that make use of phishing emails and fake hiring portals like BlockNovas, AccuraSoftHire ("accurasofthire[.]com") and HuntRole ("huntrole[.]org") to trick prospective targets into running malware-laced projects under the pretext of a take-home assessment. - Publishing malicious packages across open-source ecosystems by hijacking maintainer accounts to plant obfuscated malware through fake font files (fa-solid-400.woff2, fa-solid-500.woff2, or fa-solid-300.llf), Visual Studio Code (VS Code) auto-run tasks, and Git history rewriting. - Using compromised developer machines to steal their GitHub tokens and force-push malicious commits into open-source repositories they have access to. At a high level, the PolinRider loader retrieves an encrypted second-stage Node.js payload that scans the infected host for installed developer applications, such as GitHub Desktop, Cursor, VS Code, and Google Antigravity, and tampers with the most frequently used tools to execute attacker-controlled code and deliver infostealer malware. It's worth noting here that PolinRider is assessed to be a sub-cluster operating in parallel with a long-running campaign codenamed Contagious Interview. While the latter is more of a social-engineering entry point that's used to compromise developer systems, PolinRider abuses the access to modify repositories and turn them into a distribution channel for malware. "Cybercriminal groups deploy supply chain worms for opportunistic theft. On the other hand, North Korean state-sponsored threat actors use open-source software registries as a primary initial access vector targeting corporate environments," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said in a report published last month. "Threat actors demonstrate how compromising a single maintainer account or registry scope converts open-source dependencies, resulting in widespread affected cloud environments." Some of the decoy sites have been found to incorporate two other alternate delivery paths - - Instruct candidates to sideload a Google Chrome extension after enabling "Developer mode" to subscribe to new job alerts. - Employ ClickFix-style lures to get victims to copy and paste malicious commands into the terminal app depending on the operating system as part of a "standard settings bundle for candidates and interview workflows." "The [job] application asks for a short verification video," StepSecurity said. "Until the server marks a candidate as having installed a 'driver,' the camera check always fails with a message saying the system does not have a compatible camera environment." "A separate 'Technical onboarding' page on the site gives a one-line curl command to download the 'driver.' On Windows, the downloaded installer fetches a script from the careers site that installs Node.js if it is missing, downloads a JavaScript payload, runs it in the background and deletes itself. The macOS and Linux versions do the same." The JavaScript malware is designed to perform the following steps - - Read the latest transaction associated with an Ethereum wallet ("0xa322E5f3D311D3080e6f0121063e9aDC2490Ef1a"). - Get its destination wallet address ("0x67B38e9b67B38E9b68656c6C6f6970626f742121"). - Extract the C2 server address twice ("103.179.142[.]155") from the first eight bytes ("67B38e9b" and "67B38E9b") of the wallet address, using a technique referred to as NullReceiver, while the last 12 bytes represent the ASCII string "helloipbot!!." - Use the IP address to fetch two payloads, "0x/cls" and "0x/ls," over port 443. The latest findings from SafeDep show that the repositories are injected with a 58-line Python loader that reads the "0x3b1574417524c11a7403c4b232CAcBb320CceBC6" wallet to extract JavaScript code that then reaches out to a second wallet ("0x1eEf0849EDa15d87f64e51C73C8442Cf3c8bCEF3") to obtain the destination wallet associated with the latest transaction ("0x5F87b5545F87b55468656C6C6f6970626f742121"), which is then used to parse the C2 server ("95.135.181[.]84"). A defining aspect of NullReceiver is the marker "68656c6C6f6970626f742121" in the made-up destination wallet address that consistently translates to "helloipbot!!." "The /0x/cls script runs twice, once with eval in the current process and once in a new process," SafeDep said. "The /0x/ls script runs only in a new process." The exact nature of these payloads remains unknown. However, prior waves have been observed installing a stealer that harvests environment secrets, browser passwords, cookies, and wallet data. Interestingly, the wallet address "0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3" has been reused by the threat actors across other attack waves - - Pushing compromised versions of legitimate npm packages such as @adminide-stack/utils, @adminide-stack/health-api-server, @adminide-stack/user-activity-browser, @adminide-stack/utils, @adminide-stack/forms-core, @adminide-stack/yantra-help-browser, server-hemera-mongo, cdeops, @cdmbase/wiki-browser, and @pubngo-stack/help-browser that use the same wallet address to fetch /0x/cls and /0x/ls from "95.135.181[.]151." - A fake recruitment campaign from HuntRole that convinces victims to complete a coding assessment, which uses a VS Code extension named "huntrole.assessment-tool" from the Visual Studio Marketplace to send system information and fetch and run a malicious JavaScript payload. The script queries the same wallet address to fetch /0x/cls and /0x/ls from "95.135.181[.]84." - Using a GitHub account named " Eternity0207 " to open over 200 pull requests targeting open-source projects like AsyncAPI Generator, CircuitVerse, and Open Food Facts, and subsequently force-push a modified commit containing an obfuscated loader that uses the same wallet address to fetch /0x/cls and /0x/ls from "95.135.181[.]84." - According to the maintainer of AsyncAPI Generator, "Each time, the payload stayed on the branch for 30-40 minutes and was then force-pushed away, so the final diff looked clean." The unauthorized modifications allowed the loader to run when an unsuspecting developer runs "npm run build" (for AsyncAPI), loads the test configuration (for Open Food Facts), or opens the folder in VS Code (for CircuitVerse). The GitHub account has since been suspended. According to estimates from Apiiro, PolinRider has been detected in at least 7,609 GitHub repos owned by 2,330 accounts, most of them belonging to developers. Some of the victims include Neutralinojs, InstaWP Connect, and fxhash. The loader has been pushed to 2,040 repositories between October 27 and November 6, 2026. "The worm uses stolen GitHub access to rewrite commits the developer already made, keeping the author, message and date, and adds a loader hidden after hundreds of spaces in a build config," Apiiro researcher Shmulik Cohen said. "Building the project runs it. In the newest wave, opening the folder in VS Code is enough. The loader reads its server from an Ethereum wallet, so taking a server down changes nothing: one transaction moves every loader to the next." The development comes as OpenSourceMalware said it discovered a PolinRider attack from May 2025, predating the earliest documented victims by eight months. The attack targeted nine packages, using hijacked maintainer account to push poisoned versions within a span of 90 minutes - - itsa-utils@1.4.2 - itsa-jsext@2.0.3 - itsa-react-docviewer@16.1.2 - itsa-cli@16.5.3 - itsa-react-button@16.0.11 - itsa-react-maskedinput@16.1.2 - itsa-react-checkbox@16.0.5 - itsa-react-focuscontainer@16.0.10 - itsa-react-input@16.1.2 Each of these packages have been found to leverage EtherHiding, a precursor to NullReceiver, to retrieve a JavaScript downloader called JADESNOW, which is then used to deliver InvisibleFerret, a Python-based backdoor used in Contagious Interview campaigns, along with a Socket.IO RAT and a Python-based stealer. "The 2025 sample carries PolinRider's payload but not its documented spread behavior, which appears in the same maintainer's GitHub repositories in four windows between January and July 2026," security researchers Paul McCarty and Jenn Gile said. "The blockchain records behind it date attacker activity back to February 2025." "The infection likely persisted on the maintainer's machine from 2025, because the 2026 pushes ran from it. That matches PolinRider's documented propagation script, which rolls back the clock, folds the payload into the tip commit, and force-pushes with the developer's own credentials."
history.summary: North Korea-linked PolinRider campaign has planted a Python loader in over 7,600 GitHub repositories, which reads Ethereum wallet transaction data to decode and execute JavaScript malware that fetches command-and-control server addresses and delivers infostealer payloads. The loader spreads by hijacking maintainer accounts, rewriting commits with hidden build-config entries, and triggering when developers run builds or open projects in VS Code, with the wallet address "0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3" reused across multiple attack waves. Fix: Security researchers recommend verifying maintainer account integrity, auditing Git history for unauthorized force-pushes, and monitoring Ethereum wallet transactions linked to repository loads for suspicious decoder activity.

history.title: 1Password Hacked, Customer Data and Source Code Stolen in GitHub Account Breach
history.text: Popular password management software 1Password on Wednesday disclosed a security incident involving its backend systems that led to the unauthorized access of some customer information, but emphasized that customer password vaults and other secrets were not accessed. "While we took immediate steps to contain the incident, the attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and accessed a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including names and email addresses," the Toronto-based company said. It noted that no customer vault content, including secrets, passwords, and other vault items, account recovery keys, or the keys that secure them, was accessed or compromised as a result of the breach. It also stated that customers do not need to take any action, but cautioned them to stay vigilant against unexpected phishing attempts. As part of its efforts to remediate the incident, 1Password has disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, hardened GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, restored clean versions of the affected service, and rotated internal credentials. It has also lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure. According to the company, the incident dates back to November 19, 2026, when it began investigating suspicious activity after an unknown threat actor gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account. The attacker is said to have weaponized the account to access source code and push malicious code to its backend services, resulting in the download of administrative data related to its customers, including - - Names - Email addresses - Account and user identifiers, such as account creation and last sign-in times - Public keys - Secure Remote Password protocol parameters - Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning, and account recovery - Non-secret internal metadata about the account, such as version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers 1Password also noted that the tokens embedded in the links cannot be used on their own to gain access to customer accounts, as doing so requires either single sign-on (SSO) authentication or a six-digit verification code sent to the user's registered email address. However, it noted that a small number of users were affected and have been individually notified. "The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system," 1Password said. "Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. There is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security." "Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers."
history.summary: 1Password disclosed a security incident where an attacker gained access to an employee's corporate GitHub account, used it to access backend systems, and downloaded limited customer account information including names, email addresses, account identifiers, public keys, and Secure Remote Password protocol parameters. The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to the CI/CD system, but 1Password confirmed that no customer vault secrets, passwords, or encryption keys were accessed or compromised. Fix: 1Password disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, hardened GitHub CI/CD and endpoint controls, restored clean versions of the affected service, rotated internal credentials, and lengthened codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.

history.title: 1Password Breach Exposes Customer Data, Internal Source Code
history.text: Password management and identity security company 1Password revealed on Wednesday that a hacker stole customer information and proprietary source code. 1Password says customer vaults are not affected. The company launched an investigation on November 19 after discovering that an employee’s corporate GitHub account may have been compromised. The attacker used the account to deploy malicious code to backend services and exfiltrate customer records. The compromised customer records include names, email addresses, account identifiers, public cryptographic keys, authentication parameters, account activity times, and non-secret metadata. In addition, the threat actor obtained source code from private repositories and accessed the company’s CI/CD system, potentially exposing infrastructure credentials. According to 1Password, the hacker also obtained tokens from emails sent to users for account invitations, provisioning, and recovery. A “small number” of individuals who were undergoing provisioning or recovery during the intrusion have been notified. However, the company noted that the exposed tokens cannot be exploited on their own and there is no evidence that the attacker hijacked user accounts. A 1Password representative noted on the company’s community forum that the stolen authentication data included Secure Remote Password verifiers derived from user account passwords and Secret Keys. The verifiers cannot be used directly for authentication, and brute-forcing account passwords would require the associated Secret Keys, which 1Password does not store. 1Password highlighted that customer vaults and the cryptographic keys protecting them were not compromised. “We have no evidence that encrypted vaults were downloaded or accessed,” a 1Password community manager said. The breach also does not impact client applications, browser extensions, and account recovery keys. It’s unclear how many users are affected and how the hacker gained initial access to the corporate GitHub account. In response to the intrusion, 1Password disabled the compromised GitHub account, invalidated a stolen token, replaced potentially compromised infrastructure credentials, and restored clean versions of affected services. The company said its investigation, conducted with independent cybersecurity experts, is still ongoing. Customers do not need to take any action, but have been advised to watch for phishing attacks that could exploit news of the incident. history.summary: 1Password breach revealed that a hacker stole customer data and source code after compromising an employee's corporate GitHub account, deploying malicious code to backend services and exfiltrating records containing names, emails, account identifiers, public cryptographic keys, authentication parameters, and metadata. The attacker also accessed private source code and the CI/CD system, potentially exposing infrastructure credentials, while obtaining tokens from invitation and recovery emails; 1Password confirmed customer vaults and cryptographic keys protecting them were not compromised. In response, the company disabled the compromised GitHub account, invalidated the stolen token, replaced potentially compromised infrastructure credentials, and restored clean versions of affected services.

history.title: Fake paid expert interviews impersonate brands to steal Google logins
history.text: An ongoing phishing campaign dubbed "GoodGuys" impersonates major brands, including Google, Nvidia, Accenture, and SpaceX, to steal corporate Google and Okta credentials using fake invitations to paid expert interviews and webinars. The attacks offer recipients up to $600 for a 45-minute interview in an attempt to get them to sign in with their work accounts to participate. The campaign was discovered by cybersecurity firm Push Security, which has tracked it since October 13 and found that they impersonate eight companies: Accenture, American Express, Coca-Cola, Culver's, Google Cloud, Nvidia, SpaceX, and Spotify. The threat actors abuse legitimate email and event platforms, including HireVue, SendGrid, Mandrill, and Cvent, to distribute phishing links. In one attack, a phishing email sent through HireVue invited recipients to attend a Google Cloud webinar about deploying AI applications into production. The threat actors use domains themed around interviews, webinars, and research studies, creating brand-specific subdomains to host the phishing pages, such as: - accenture[.]international-interviews[.]com - nvidia[.]feedback-study[.]com - google[.]webinar-cloud[.]com - spotify[.]interview-experts[.]com Clicking the phishing links typically takes recipients to a CAPTCHA challenge before displaying a website impersonating the company that supposedly sent the invitation. Each website features customized branding and lures, with the Nvidia phishing site offering $500 to participate in an AI feedback study and the Accenture site offering $600 for an expert interview. The sites ultimately prompt visitors to sign in with their Google accounts to validate their invitations, allowing the attackers to steal their credentials. The phishing kit specifically targets corporate accounts and rejects email addresses associated with Gmail, Yahoo, and Outlook. Unlike adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing kits that use reverse proxies to relay legitimate login pages, GoodGuys uses fake authentication forms controlled by an attacker-controlled server. After victims enter their Google credentials, the phishing page can display various multifactor authentication (MFA) challenges, including requests for SMS codes, authenticator codes, and Google sign-in prompts requiring users to select a matching number on their phones. The kit also includes fake Okta authentication forms and support for Okta Verify push notifications. Push Security believes the threat actors manually attempt to log in using the stolen credentials, instructing the phishing page to display whatever MFA or security challenges Google or Okta show during authentication. Similar techniques were used in vishing-based data theft attacks linked to the ShinyHunters extortion gang earlier this year to steal corporate single sign-on (SSO) credentials. Once the process is completed, the phishing kit redirects victims to another website or displays a message thanking them for their application. The researchers believe the phishing kit may have been developed using an AI coding assistant, based on hidden accessibility labels found in every analyzed version of the kit. "The sign-in card in every build carries two hidden labels: "Sign-in simulation" and "GoodGuys sign-in simulation." They sit in accessibility text that only screen readers announce, so a visitor never sees them. We think the label is a leftover from how the kit was first built," explained Push Security. "Calling the page a sign-in "simulation" for a made-up company is the kind of framing someone would use to get an AI coding assistant past its guardrails when asking it to build a phishing page. The label then stayed in every build we've collected." The researchers also discovered a potentially related phishing campaign that uses fake Coca-Cola interview invitations and the Evilginx phishing kit to target Google Ads accounts. While both campaigns used the same abused SendGrid click tracker and identical Coca-Cola branding assets, differences in their code and infrastructure prevented researchers from conclusively linking the attacks to the same threat actor. history.title: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
history.text: CISA Adds Three Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog CISA has added three new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. - CVE-2026-120705 OSGeo GeoServer XML Injection Vulnerability - CVE-2026-129243 OSGeo GeoServer Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability - CVE-2026-136716 Drupal Core Improper Check for Unusual or Exceptional Conditions Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance. history.title: Suspected Vietnam-Linked Hackers Target Southeast Asia in South China Sea Espionage Campaign
history.text: A Vietnam-sponsored hacking group has been attributed to attacks targeting Southeast Asian military, government, and legislative organizations with an aim to gather intelligence on South China Sea defense and military agreements. The previously undocumented incursion set, detailed by SOCRadar, has been codenamed WeaveLotus. The activity is assessed to have comprised five intrusions in Thailand and the Philippines and reconnaissance efforts against Indonesian government organizations. "Initial access was achieved primarily by exploiting web application vulnerabilities and default credentials in open-source software, including GeoServer, JasperReports, osTicket, and exposed Laravel debug mode configurations," SOCRadar said in an analysis published Thursday. "The threat actor established persistent internal network access using reverse SSH tunnels and moved laterally into downstream networks and applications." The links to Vietnam are based on the presence of native Vietnamese-language code comments, operational activity aligning with UTC+07:00 working hours, regional strategic targeting, and custom scripting. The sustained campaign, codenamed RedOps, was observed between August and September 2026. The threat actor has also been observed conducting open-source intelligence (OSINT), setting up automated Bing search scripts that scraped news and documents on military agreements involving the Philippines, China, and the U.S., with a particular emphasis on the South China Sea, a region of strategic and geopolitical importance. Earlier this August, Hunt.io disclosed details of another cyber espionage operation undertaken by a suspected Chinese threat actor targeting a nuclear research organization and a marine engineering and shipbuilding company to steal sensitive documents after gaining access through known security vulnerabilities. "Following the OSINT phase, the operators enumerated government, military, and legislative entities across the Philippines, Thailand, and Indonesia, compromising targets in Thailand and the Philippines across five confirmed intrusions," SOCRadar said. "Activity against Indonesian targets did not progress beyond reconnaissance." "The core objective of RedOps appears to be the exfiltration of internal records and documents from Southeast Asian governments in support of Vietnam's foreign policy and military intelligence priorities." A brief overview of the intrusion activity is as follows - - Thai military organization, which likely involved the exploitation of a critical GeoServer flaw (CVE-2024-36401, CVSS score: 9.8) to deploy a SOCKS5 proxy and open a reverse SSH tunnel, followed by hands-on reconnaissance, persistence, and unauthenticated access to Directus CMS API's file collection and asset download endpoints to enumerate records and download a subset of those records. The threat actor also ran Optical Character Recognition (OCR) on the collected data to extract English and Thai text from PNG images, and unsuccessfully attempted to gain access to surveillance video feeds hosted on Wowza to possibly gain real-time visibility into military operations. - Thai legislative organization, which involved the attacker leveraging an exposed JasperReports server with default administrative credentials (jasperadmin:jasperadmin) to upload a malicious report that ultimately executed SQL scripts on the backend Microsoft SQL Server and then deleted the report to cover up the tracks. The SQL commands, in turn, employed xp_cmdshell to launch a reverse SSH SOCKS proxy tunnel over port 443 to WeaveLotus infrastructure ("172.235.245[.]49"). The attackers deployed a lightweight Python C2 server to automate post-exploitation and targeted a third-party document management system (DMS) by launching password spraying attacks using real employee names paired with National ID numbers as passwords. Once authenticated, the attackers collected the entire system configuration, the complete application user directory comprising 1,502 records), along with system audit logs and 5,000 ZIP archives containing sensitive data. - Thai government organization, which involved the attacker gaining root SSH access to a server running Keycloak 3.4 and dumping its credential database, following cracking the PBKDF2-SHA256 hashes offline with wordlists built around Thai Buddhist Era years and then validating them in real-time against the Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) token endpoint. The working accounts belonged to users from various Thai ministries and agencies, with two of them granting the attackers administrative privileges. The valid credentials were then used to pull 349,782 records from a downstream application that contained national strategy alignment, reform directives, masterplan targets, sustainable development goals, and five-year fiscal plans, among others. - Philippine government organization A, which involved the exploitation of an unauthenticated SQL injection flaw in osTicket (CVE-2021-42235, CVSS score: 9.8) to extract database schemas and dump usernames, email addresses, and bcrypt password hashes for registered staff accounts. - Philippine government organization B, which probed a web application built on the Laravel framework to obtain server paths and fragments of application source code, ultimately revealing directories tied to an internal project-management and budgeting system. "WeaveLotus conducted broad reconnaissance against Indonesian government agencies [between August and September 2026]," SOCRadar said. "The operators began with passive reconnaissance, harvesting Certificate Transparency (CT) logs via CertSpotter and crt.sh, before progressing to active Nmap port scans, VPN service fingerprinting (targeting Palo Alto GlobalProtect, Ivanti Connect Secure / Pulse Secure, Cisco ASA, and Fortinet FortiGate), and IMAP/POP3 banner grabbing across more than 30 organizations." The RedOps campaign is notable for the fact that it has only singled out government, military, and legislative institutions in the Philippines, Thailand, and Indonesia, with no evidence that private-sector entities were targeted. This indicates that the activity is consistent with state-directed intelligence collection. "The RedOps campaign illustrates how a suspected Vietnam-linked espionage operation leveraged exposed applications, weak authentication controls, and persistent network tunnels to conduct intelligence collection across Southeast Asian government and military environments," SOCRadar said. "The recovered tooling and operational artifacts provide valuable insight into the actor's methods, while the available evidence supports tracking WeaveLotus as a distinct activity cluster without conclusively establishing state sponsorship."
history.summary: A Vietnam-sponsored hacking group dubbed WeaveLotus conducted a sustained espionage campaign (RedOps, Aug–Sep 2026) targeting Southeast Asian government, military, and legislative organizations in Thailand, the Philippines, and Indonesia to collect intelligence on South China Sea defense agreements. Initial access was achieved by exploiting web application vulnerabilities and default credentials in open-source software such as GeoServer, osTicket, and JasperReports, with persistent access established via reverse SSH tunnels and lateral movement into downstream networks.

history.title: Hex Package Manager Warns of Potential Data Breach
history.text: Hex, the package manager for Elixir and Erlang, fell victim to a cyberattack involving unauthorized access to its web servers. The incident occurred on November 23, when the attackers exploited a vulnerability in hex.pm to execute commands. The attack was immediately blocked, and the underlying security defect was addressed within 20 minutes. Between 18:16 and 18:29 UTC, the attacker sent 69 malicious requests, affecting six web servers. At 18:30, Hex replaced all hex.pm servers with patched versions rejecting the payload, and its firewall rule fully blocked the attacker’s traffic at 18:33. “We found no evidence of unauthorized package modifications, database changes, or that the attacker maintained access to our systems,” the package manager explains. According to Hex, potential access to database contents, such as email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, sessions, second factor authentication secrets, and audit logs, cannot be ruled out. While all the observed reads of private packages came from Hex servers, any read from a compromised server would appear legitimate, it says. Additionally, database and private documentation reads are not logged, hindering visibility into potential data exposure. “The attacker’s commands could read the credentials our servers use, so we replaced them: the storage, CDN, email and database credentials, and the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. This logged everyone out of hex.pm and Hex clients,” Hex notes. The package manager has been working on a new registry signing system with key rotation support. Until new Hex client iterations are rolled out, users should avoid fetching packages from third-party mirrors and rely only on repo.hex.pm. Hex also recommends that all account holders change their hex.pm passwords and reset their two-factor authentication. “Because email addresses may have been exposed, be careful with emails that claim to come from Hex. Please double-check that the links they contain lead to hex.pm,” the package manager says. The attackers exploited an unauthenticated deserialization of untrusted data bug (tracked as CVE-2026-129514, CVSS score of 10) that allowed them to execute OS commands via a crafted Erlang external term format request body and gain remote code execution (RCE). Hex discovered that the Ash Framework was also impacted by the same class of vulnerability. Ash patched the flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-124283) on November 24, warning it could lead to code execution or SQL injection. Associated security defects were also patched in two other Elixir libraries: namely db_connection (CVE-2026-133555) and flop (CVE-2026-130411). history.summary: Hex, the package manager for Elixir and Erlang, suffered a cyberattack on November 23 when attackers exploited an unauthenticated deserialization vulnerability (CVE-2026-129514, CVSS 10) in hex.pm to execute OS commands and gain remote code execution via crafted Erlang external term format requests. Between 18:16 and 18:29 UTC, the attacker sent 69 malicious requests affecting six web servers before Hex replaced all servers with patched versions at 18:30 and fully blocked the traffic with a firewall rule at 18:33.

history.title: pCloud confirms password manager hack after suspicious login alerts
history.text: The pCloud Pass password manager suffered a cyberattack, with users reporting that unknown devices had connected to their accounts even with two-factor authentication (2FA) enabled. The incident was first reported by numerous pCloud customers who began receiving email notifications informing them that a new device had connected to their pCloud Pass accounts. In two Reddit threads, customers worldwide reported receiving notifications warning that an unfamiliar device named "pd" connected to their account from the IP address 45.131.244.7 in Luxembourg, which users say belongs to pCloud's own infrastructure. Several customers reported receiving the alerts despite having two-factor authentication (2FA) enabled on their accounts. However, when customers checked their accounts for connected devices, some found no unfamiliar devices listed. Other pCloud customers reported receiving the same notifications despite never having used the company's password manager, including one who said the notification was sent to an email address associated with a pCloud storage account they had requested be deleted almost a year ago. In response to the reports, pCloud confirmed its password manager had suffered a cyberattack, which the company says was quickly contained. "A cyberattack targeting pCloud Pass occurred, which was promptly contained by the pCloud team," reads pCloud's statement. "Unfortunately, a small number of pCloud Pass user email addresses were exposed and login attempts were made. Our system sends a notification automatically to each of these addresses." pCloud says the attack was isolated to its password manager and that its cloud storage services were not affected. The company says that passwords, notes, and other information stored in pCloud Pass have not been compromised, explaining that the data is encrypted on customers' devices and can only be decrypted using their master passwords. However, pCloud did not disclose whether any encrypted password vaults were accessed or stolen during the attack. This matters because threat actors who obtain encrypted password vaults could try to crack them offline without being subject to the service's login rate limits or two-factor authentication protections. This was demonstrated in the 2022 LastPass breach, when attackers stole backups containing encrypted password vaults. Researchers later linked the breach to cryptocurrency thefts in which attackers are believed to have cracked weak or reused master passwords to access stored cryptocurrency wallet private keys and seed phrases. A reader who contacted BleepingComputer also noted that the "Open settings" link in the email notifications pointed to passqa1.pcloud.com, which appears to be a quality assurance (QA) environment rather than the password manager's production website. BleepingComputer confirmed that the link pointed to the same hostname in a copy of the notification shared with us. In its statement, pCloud also discussed how advancements in artificial intelligence are accelerating the discovery of software vulnerabilities, but did not specifically state that this was an AI-powered attack. The company is also warning customers to watch for phishing attacks, stating that it will never ask for their master passwords or recovery words over email, phone, or chat. The pCloud Pass incident is the latest in a series of cyberattacks impacting password managers this month. Earlier in November, mSeven Software warned mSecure customers to change stored passwords, reset two-factor authentication, and remove passkeys after a hacker reportedly stole an encrypted customer database. On Wednesday, 1Password disclosed a data breach after a threat actor compromised an employee's GitHub account and deployed malicious code to the company's backend services to steal customer data. However, 1Password said customers' password vaults and the encryption keys protecting them were not compromised. Uncover email threats your existing defenses may miss. The company confirmed the attack was contained, stating that a small number of user email addresses were exposed and automatic login notifications were sent, while emphasizing that stored passwords and encrypted data remain protected by master passwords. pCloud also warned customers to watch for phishing, noting it will never ask for master passwords or recovery words via email, phone, or chat.

history.title: New Boston Scientific data breach exposes personal, medical info
history.text: Medical technology company Boston Scientific is sending data breach notices to individuals affected by a cyberattack on the firm. According to a notification sample Boston Scientific shared with U.S. authorities, the hacker used social engineering in a voice phishing (vishing) attack to gain access to the company's cloud infrastructure. The attack exposed cloud-based applications and cloud-hosted data between May 7 and 1. The company became aware of the unauthorized access on May 12, and the investigation determined that a data breach occurred on November 5. Individuals in multiple U.S. states have been impacted, exposing personal details and medical information. According to the Texas Attorney General breach portal, the incident exposed information from 117,789 people, which included: - Full name - Physical address - Social Security Number (SSN) - Government-issued ID number (e.g., passport, state ID card) - Medical information - Health insurance information - Date of birth The letter sent to impacted individuals specifies that patient medical records and data from remote monitoring systems, connected medical devices, and clinical case management or workflow applications were not exposed. Boston Scientific is a Massachusetts-based medical device maker whose products include stents, catheters, pacemakers, defibrillators, and endoscopes. It is one of the world’s largest medical device manufacturers, with more than 59,000 employees, 13 manufacturing facilities, and a presence in 127 countries. In 2025, Boston Scientific reported more than $20 billion in revenue. The company said there was no disruption to manufacturing, ordering, distribution, or service to patients and healthcare providers as a result of this incident. It also said the incident had no impact on operations, performance, remote monitoring, or the safety of its products and medical devices. Boston Scientific says it contained the incident, investigated with outside cybersecurity experts, and notified law enforcement. The notification does not offer free credit monitoring to impacted individuals but recommends using free credit reports and considering placing fraud alerts and credit freezes. Second breach in 2026 The breach is the second cybersecurity incident this year. On August 25, Boston Scientific disclosed a cyberattack that caused network outages and a global operational disruption for the company, including to order processing and shipping. CrowdStrike’s investigation determined that the attacker breached an internet-facing network device and pivoted to a limited part of the on-premises IT environment. However, the investigators found no evidence that the attackers compromised cloud applications. BleepingComputer contacted Boston Scientific to learn more about the most recent incident, and a spokesperson confirmed that it is unrelated to the August 2026 intrusion. history.title: US Air Force cloud platform reportedly hacked in latest federal breach
history.text: Hackers have reportedly breached the US Air Force's Cloud One computing platform, adding to a recent wave of cyberattacks affecting US government agencies, including the FBI, CIA, and Treasury Department. According to Reuters, the intrusion was discovered within the past month during an upgrade of the cloud platform, disrupting application migrations and software updates. Launched in 2017, Cloud One is an enterprise cloud computing platform managed by the US Air Force that allows Department of Defense agencies to host and manage applications supporting military operations, personnel management, logistics, and maintenance. According to one source who spoke to Reuters, the hackers exploited an unidentified software vulnerability to gain access to the platform, potentially exposing sensitive military operational and logistics information. US Cyber Command has reportedly been called in to assess the impact, with the attackers, scope of the attack, and whether any data was stolen currently unknown. The Air Force declined to comment on the security or operational status of the affected systems, telling Reuters that it continuously takes measures to protect its information, systems, and mission capabilities. The reported Air Force breach follows other cybersecurity incidents disclosed over the past week targeting US federal agencies. On November 21, it was revealed that hackers reportedly breached the FBI's National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a nationwide database used by local, state, and federal law enforcement agencies. The database contains information on wanted and missing persons, outstanding arrest warrants, stolen vehicles and firearms, and other criminal justice records. The intrusion came two months after the ShinyHunters extortion group breached FBI systems by exploiting an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft vulnerability in the agency's recruitment website, FBIJobs.gov. Earlier this week, hackers also reportedly breached an open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis system at the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). The incident also affected the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) and the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA). Hours after the CIA breach was reported, the US Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed that it was investigating unauthorized access to its systems. It is unclear whether any of the recently disclosed federal government breaches are connected. AI-powered hacking tools fuel cyberattacks The CIA breach was reportedly conducted using the ARTEX AI-powered penetration testing platform, which the FBI recently warned was being used to automate cyberattacks worldwide. In an advisory, the FBI said multiple threat actors had used ARTEX since at least August 2026 in attacks targeting government, defense, healthcare, financial, and technology organizations. ARTEX is an open-source penetration testing framework that uses AI agents to automate various stages of a cyberattack, including discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities, escalating privileges, and stealing data. The framework integrates with external AI models from Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, DeepSeek, Grok, and others, allowing attackers to conduct autonomous attacks against organizations with minimal human intervention. According to the FBI, some ARTEX-powered intrusions have progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. The platform was used by a Chinese state-aligned threat actor tracked by Microsoft as Storm-0940 in an October attack targeting ConnectWise's Cloud Backup service. Cybersecurity firm Huntress identified at least 162 compromised Microsoft 365 customer tenants during the campaign. Other attacks linked to ARTEX include: - Attacks against South Korean financial institutions that exposed personal information of approximately 67,000 people. - A South Korean hacking campaign targeting more than 90 organizations, resulting in the theft of approximately 8.2 million data records and the arrest of seven suspects. - A cyberespionage campaign attributed by CrowdStrike to a Chinese hacking group tracked as Vapor Panda, which targeted more than 200 organizations across 14 countries and compromised at least nine. As of early November, researchers had identified more than 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX management consoles, with the number believed to be much higher. The intrusion was discovered within the past month during a cloud platform upgrade, disrupting application migrations and software updates, and hackers exploited an unidentified software vulnerability, potentially exposing sensitive military operational and logistics information. history.title: In Other News: Tanker Cyberattacks, EU Quantum Act, New VirusTotal Capabilities
history.text: SecurityWeek’s weekly cybersecurity news roundup offers a concise overview of important developments that may not receive full standalone coverage yet remain relevant to the broader threat landscape. This curated summary highlights key stories across vulnerability disclosures, emerging attack methods, policy updates, industry reports, and other noteworthy events to help readers stay well-informed about the evolving cybersecurity environment. Here are this week’s highlights: ChatGPT Sites exposure Pluto researchers combed web archives, public code repositories, search engines and other sources and found 16,666 sites created with ChatGPT Sites (which builds and hosts web apps for ChatGPT and Codex users), 12,830 of which were accessible to anyone. Manual checks confirmed sensitive data exposure at 27 organizations, including a Fortune 500 company’s sales dashboard, a freight forwarder’s customer quotes, and a vendor’s sales pitch. Sites are visible only to their owners and admins unless shared, but owners can open them to the entire internet. RansomwareHelp co-founder accused of profiting from ransom payments US authorities have charged Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, a Colombian national and co-founder of the ransomware recovery firm RansomwareHelp, with three counts of wire fraud. Prosecutors allege that instead of using its own decryption technology as advertised, his company purchased decryptors from cybercriminals at prices significantly lower than what it charged customers. In one case involving undercover FBI agents, Palacio allegedly paid a $6,000 ransom and billed the purported victim $13,260 for decrypting their files. USDA payment systems breach A system used by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) to make payments to farmers has been breached, according to NBC News. Two former department officials said the intrusion could let hackers access databases containing sensitive information on food safety and diseases carried by animals. SolarWinds and Adobe patch vulnerabilities SolarWinds has patched several critical vulnerabilities in its Serv-U managed file transfer product, including flaws that can lead to privilege escalation and arbitrary code execution. Adobe has addressed critical security holes in Campaign Classic and Experience Manager, including ones that allow arbitrary code execution, and a medium-severity DoS vulnerability in InDesign. Container Store restores systems after cyberattack US retailer The Container Store has restored its systems following a cyberattack that prevented customers from placing orders online. There is currently no evidence that customers’ financial information was stolen. The n0n ransomware group listed the company on its leak site earlier this month, but The Container Store has not addressed the claim. VirusTotal adds new ransomware detection capabilities VirusTotal has introduced new ransomware detection capabilities that rely on evidence of user files being encrypted during sandbox analysis. The improvements include a new behavior tag and stricter requirements for assigning the MITRE ATT&CK technique associated with data encryption for impact. VirusTotal demonstrated the effectiveness of the changes against ransomware that evaded detection by all 75 static antivirus engines at the time of analysis. $17 billion targeted in US government anti-scam operation The US Justice Department’s crackdown on fraud has targeted more than 800 defendants across over 400 cases since March. Authorities have also helped disrupt scam centers in more than 10 countries. According to the FBI, its Operation Blackout has led to the seizure or restraint of nearly $17 billion. McDonald’s Japan hacked McDonald’s Japan has disclosed a breach involving a database storing information associated with its mobile application. Hackers gained access to customer purchase histories, device location information, internal customer identifiers and IP addresses, but not names, contact details or credit card data. The number of impacted customers has not been disclosed. Bithumb uncovers wider breach South Korean cryptocurrency exchange Bithumb says more individuals and more types of personal information were compromised in an October cyberattack than initially reported. Bithumb also said the hackers had access for more than two weeks, not one hour as initially believed. The hackers stole data from an internal collaboration system, including identity documents, bank account numbers, transaction histories, and crypto wallet addresses. South Korean media reported that the initial victim count exceeded 7,000, including customers and staff. Artex gains traction among state-sponsored hackers Microsoft has observed several state-sponsored hacking groups, including China’s Salt Typhoon, as well as cybercriminals using the AI-powered penetration testing framework Artex. Hackers have leveraged the tool to identify exposed secrets in public code repositories, conduct supply chain attacks and find vulnerable systems. Microsoft says the framework can significantly accelerate intrusions, with attackers achieving privileged access and establishing persistence within minutes. Quantum Act targets Europe’s cryptographic readiness The European Commission’s proposed Quantum Act includes measures to accelerate the development and adoption of post-quantum cryptography and prepare the EU for the security risks posed by quantum computers. The legislation is part of a broader effort to strengthen Europe’s quantum technology industry, reduce reliance on foreign suppliers and establish global leadership in the field by 2030. Tanker cyberattacks Up to 50 ships carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemicals and other potentially dangerous cargo are believed to have been targeted in a wave of cyberattacks, according to The Wall Street Journal. US authorities are investigating whether Iran is responsible for the attacks. Radware hacked An internal report obtained by BleepingComputer shows that hackers breached cybersecurity firm Radware through an unprotected Cloud WAF management API exposed to the internet. Customer contact information and credentials associated with AWS, Azure and SFTP storage used by some customers may have been compromised. The company has not responded to SecurityWeek’s request for comment. history.summary: Cybersecurity researchers found 16,666 ChatGPT Sites created, with 12,830 accessible to the public, exposing sensitive data at 27 organizations including a Fortune 500 sales dashboard. US prosecutors charged the co-founder of RansomwareHelp with wire fraud for allegedly buying decryptors cheap and charging customers far more. The USDA confirmed a breach of its farmer payment system that could expose sensitive food safety and animal disease databases.

history.title: SAP confirms security incident after suspicious GitHub activity
history.text: SAP has confirmed to BleepingComputer that it took urgent action to protect its customers after detecting suspicious activity in its IT environment. The German software giant said its evidence so far does not show downstream compromise of customer systems or data. Based in Walldorf, Germany, SAP is one of the world’s largest enterprise software vendors, with 110,000 employees in 157 countries, 300 million subscribers, and over $40 billion in annual revenue. Der Spiegel reported earlier today, based on an internal SAP memo it saw, that the software firm was hit by a cyberattack it tracks under the code name “Project Granite.” The software company reportedly asked all employees to keep the project details confidential. According to the German outlet, sources within the company said the attackers breached SAP’s GitHub environment, possibly with help from AI tools. Insider sources say that the attacker managed to steal authentication tokens from SAP employees and leveraged them to copy and also modify SAP source code on GitHub. BleepingComputer has contacted SAP for a statement on the reported breach, and the company acknowledged the incident and said it had taken steps to protect its customers. “SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services,” a company representative told BleepingComputer. “Based on our investigation to date, we have found no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data.” “Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on.” SAP did not specify the environments where the suspicious activity was observed, or whether customers downloading code from its GitHub repositories or performing updates that are directly fetched or indirectly fed by those repositories should take any action. BleepingComputer has asked SAP about this, but a spokesperson declined to share any further information. Meanwhile, Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security (BSI) issued a public warning yesterday about agentic AI tools that empower cyberattacks, such as ARTEX, CAIRN, and PentAGI. BSI cautioned organizations in the country to focus on responding to security incidents and ensure they follow all recommended security-strengthening practices. This warning comes shortly after the national cybersecurity agencies in Switzerland and Italy reported the first detections of large-scale AI-driven cyberattacks targeting organizations in the critical infrastructure sector. history.title: 100,000 Potentially Impacted by Colorado Data Breach
history.text: The Colorado Governor’s Office of Information Technology (OIT) has disclosed a data breach impacting data that residents uploaded to the myColorado application. Colorado’s official mobile application, myColorado is used for digital identification, state services, and document storage. It has approximately 2.1 million users. OIT took the application offline last week, after identifying unauthorized access to platform data, and immediately initiated incident response and an investigation into the incident. One week after the outage began, OIT said it discovered the incident after the attackers triggered the automated threat detection systems deployed within its Amazon Web Services (AWS) environment. The investigation has determined that the attackers accessed documents stored within the ‘myCards and Documents’ section of the application, which includes user-uploaded data, such as PDF files and photos of government IDs, vehicle registrations, and insurance cards. According to Colorado, approximately 100,000 individuals might have been affected, but no payment information was accessed. “Staff are working around the clock to match the inappropriately accessed documents to individual users. As that matching continues, OIT will further refine estimates on the number of people whose data was involved,” Colorado said. The myColorado application remains offline and OIT has not announced a restoration date. The state expects to start sending direct notifications to the affected individuals on November 27. “Our main goal is to protect the security of users. Additionally, we are prioritizing direct notification of users involved in the incident and getting the app up and running as soon as possible, with security enhancements in place,” said state CIO and OIT executive director Sarah Tuneberg. history.summary: A Colorado data breach exposed user-uploaded documents in the myColorado app, including government IDs, vehicle registrations, and insurance cards, affecting approximately 100,000 of its 2.1 million users. The app was taken offline after attackers triggered automated threat detection systems in its AWS environment, and officials are matching accessed documents to individual users to refine impact estimates. Notifications to affected individuals are set to begin on November 27, with the state aiming to restore the app with enhanced security.
